## Learning goals

By the end of this lab you will be able to:

1. Perform exploratory data analysis on a multivariate dataset.
2. Fit a multiple linear regression model and interpret each coefficient as a **partial effect**.
3. Check regression assumptions with residual plots and identify violations.
4. Apply a log response transformation and verify it resolves those violations.
5. Build the ANOVA table, perform the overall $F$-test, and compute $R^2$ on the validated model.
6. Conduct $t$-tests and construct confidence intervals on the validated model.
7. Compute and interpret confidence and prediction intervals, with back-transformation to the original scale.

---

# The Data

The built-in R dataset `airquality` contains 153 daily air quality measurements collected in New York from May through September 1973. We will model **ozone concentration** as a function of three meteorological variables.

| Variable | Description | Units |
|:---------|:-----------|:------|
| `Ozone` | Mean ozone concentration | Parts per billion (ppb) |
| `Temp` | Maximum daily temperature | Degrees Fahrenheit (°F) |
| `Wind` | Average wind speed | Miles per hour (mph) |
| `Solar.R` | Solar radiation | Langleys (lang) |

```{r load-data, eval=FALSE}
data(airquality)
aq <- na.omit(airquality[, c("Ozone", "Temp", "Wind", "Solar.R")])
head(aq)
```

Calling `na.omit()` removes rows with any missing values. The cleaned dataset has 111 complete observations.

# Part 2: Fitting the Multiple Regression Model

```{r fit-model, eval=FALSE}
fit <- lm(Ozone ~ Temp + Wind + Solar.R, data = aq)

```

# Part 3: Residual Diagnostics

Before drawing any conclusions from the model, we check whether the regression assumptions hold.

```{r residual-plots, fig.height=6, eval=FALSE}
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))

plot(aq$Temp,    residuals(fit),
     xlab = "Temp (°F)",      ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs Temp",    pch = 16, col = "steelblue")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")

plot(aq$Wind,    residuals(fit),
     xlab = "Wind (mph)",     ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs Wind",    pch = 16, col = "steelblue")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")

plot(aq$Solar.R, residuals(fit),
     xlab = "Solar.R (lang)", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs Solar.R", pch = 16, col = "steelblue")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")

plot(fitted(fit), residuals(fit),
     xlab = "Fitted values",  ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs Fitted",  pch = 16, col = "steelblue")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")

qqnorm(residuals(fit), main = "Normal QQ-Plot", pch = 16, col = "steelblue")
qqline(residuals(fit), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
```

# Part 4: Applying a Log Transformation

The diagnostic plots reveal violations of equal variance and normality. Because ozone concentrations are bounded below by zero and tend to be right-skewed, a **log transformation** of the response is a natural remedy.

```{r log-residuals, fig.height=6, eval=FALSE}
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))

plot(aq$Temp,    residuals(fit_log),
     xlab = "Temp (°F)",      ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs Temp",    pch = 16, col = "darkorange")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")

plot(aq$Wind,    residuals(fit_log),
     xlab = "Wind (mph)",     ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs Wind",    pch = 16, col = "darkorange")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")

plot(aq$Solar.R, residuals(fit_log),
     xlab = "Solar.R (lang)", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs Solar.R", pch = 16, col = "darkorange")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")

plot(fitted(fit_log), residuals(fit_log),
     xlab = "Fitted values",  ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs Fitted",  pch = 16, col = "darkorange")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")

qqnorm(residuals(fit_log), main = "Normal QQ-Plot", pch = 16, col = "darkorange")
qqline(residuals(fit_log), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
```

# Part 5: ANOVA Table and Model Fit

Having verified that the log model satisfies the regression assumptions, we now conduct formal inference using `fit_log`.

```{r anova-table, eval=FALSE}
anova(fit_log)
```

The `anova()` output gives one row per predictor plus a Residuals row. It does not directly report the overall model $F^*$. To compute it manually:

1. **SSR**: sum the `Sum Sq` values across the three predictor rows (Temp, Wind, Solar.R).
2. **MSR**: divide SSR by the regression degrees of freedom, $p - 1 = 3$.
3. **MSE**: read the `Mean Sq` value from the Residuals row.
4. **$F^*$**: compute MSR / MSE.

$$F^* = \frac{\text{MSR}}{\text{MSE}} = \frac{\text{SSR} / (p-1)}{\text{MSE}}$$

```{r f-calc, eval=FALSE}
aov_out <- anova(fit_log)
SSR   <- sum(aov_out$`Sum Sq`[1:3])   # sum predictor rows
MSE   <- aov_out$`Mean Sq`[4]         # residuals row
MSR   <- SSR / 3
Fstar <- MSR / MSE
Fstar
```

# Part 7: Estimation and Prediction

Since `fit_log` models $\log(\text{Ozone})$, `predict()` returns values on the **log scale**. We apply `exp()` to back-transform to the original ppb scale.

```{r predict-new, eval=FALSE}

# Point prediction (back-transformed)
exp(predict(___, newdata = ___))

# 95% confidence interval (back-transformed)
exp(predict(___, newdata = ___, interval = ___, level = 0.95))
```
